results.question: How do you initialize a new Git repository in an existing directory?
results.expected_answer: To turn a directory into a new Git repository, you run the command git init. This command creates a .git directory where Git stores all the project's metadata and object database.
results.rtfm_answer: To initialize a new Git repository in an existing directory, navigate to the project directory and run the command `$ git init`. This creates a new `.git` subdirectory containing the necessary repository files. If you want to start version-controlling existing files, you can use `git add` to track them and `git commit` to create an initial commit. [Source 1: progit.pdf]

results.question: How do you get a copy of an existing Git repository from a server?
results.expected_answer: You use the git clone command to receive a full copy of nearly all data the server has for that project. Unlike other version control systems, Git receives every version of every file for the history of the project by default.
results.rtfm_answer:
You can get a copy of an existing Git repository from a server using the `git clone` command followed by the repository's URL. For example, to clone the Git linkable library called libgit2, you would run:

```sh
$ git clone https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2
```

This command creates a new directory named `libgit2`, initializes a `.git` directory inside it, and pulls down all the data for the repository. If you want to clone the repository into a directory with a different name, you can specify the new directory name as an additional argument:

```sh
$ git clone https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2 mylibgit
```

results.question: What command is used to check which files are in which state within your working directory?
results.expected_answer: The git status command shows you which files are modified but unstaged, which are staged for the next commit, and which are untracked. It also provides hints on how to move files between these states.
results.rtfm_answer: The git status command is used to show the different states of files in your working directory and staging area, indicating which files are modified and unstaged, and which are staged but not yet committed. [Source 4: progit.pdf (section: git status)]

results.question: How do you record staged snapshots permanently to the Git history?
results.expected_answer: The git commit command takes the files exactly as they are in the staging area and stores that snapshot permanently in the Git directory. Each commit also stores metadata such as the author's name, email, and a commit message.
results.rtfm_answer: You record staged snapshots permanently to the Git history by performing a commit. When you are ready to commit, you have selectively staged the changes you want to include in the commit. Then, you run the `git commit` command, which takes the files as they are in the staging area and stores that snapshot permanently to your Git directory. [Source 1]

results.question: What is the command to stage changes for the next commit?
results.expected_answer: The git add command adds content from the working directory into the staging area, also known as the index. This allows you to selectively craft what your next commit snapshot will look like.
results.rtfm_answer: The command to stage changes for the next commit is `git add`. This command is used to stage files that have been modified and are not yet staged.

results.question: What is the technical definition of a branch in Git?
results.expected_answer: A branch in Git is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to one of the commits in your history. The default branch name created by git init is master.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, a branch is a pointer to a specific commit in the repository history. More specifically, when you create a branch, Git creates a new pointer that initially points to the same commit as the branch it was created from. As you make commits, the branch pointer remains fixed, while the commit to which it points can have new commits added to its history. This allows you to work on different lines of development without affecting the main history of the project. [Source 1]

results.question: How do you create a new branch without switching to it?
results.expected_answer: You can create a new branch pointer using the git branch command followed by the branch name. This creates a new pointer to the same commit you are currently on.
results.rtfm_answer: To create a new branch without switching to it, you can use the `git branch` command followed by the branch name. Alternatively, you can use the shorthand `git checkout -b <branch-name>` which both creates the branch and switches to it. If you want to avoid switching branches, just use `git branch <branch-name>`. [Source 3: progit.pdf (section: **git branch**)]

results.question: How do you switch from your current branch to another existing branch?
results.expected_answer: The git checkout command is used to switch to an existing branch. When you switch branches, Git reverts the files in your working directory to look like they did the last time you committed on that branch.
results.rtfm_answer:
To switch from your current branch to another existing branch, you use the `git checkout` command followed by the name of the branch you want to switch to. For example:

```sh
$ git checkout testing
```

This command moves HEAD to point to the `testing` branch, updating your working directory to match the state of that branch at the last commit. [Source 3: Switching Branches]

results.question: What is a shortcut command to create a new branch and switch to it immediately?
results.expected_answer: You can use the git checkout command with the -b switch to create a new branch and switch to it at the same time. This is a very common operation used when starting work on a new topic or issue.
results.rtfm_answer: The shortcut command to create a new branch and switch to it immediately is `git checkout -b <branch-name>`. This command combines the actions of creating a new branch and switching to it in one step. [Source 1]

results.question: What does the special HEAD pointer represent in Git?
results.expected_answer: In Git, HEAD is a special pointer that refers to the local branch you are currently working on. It serves as the parent of the next commit you create.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, the HEAD pointer represents the current branch you are on. It is a special pointer that moves as you make new commits, always pointing to the latest commit on the current branch. [Source 2]

results.question: What happens during a fast-forward merge?
results.expected_answer: A fast-forward merge occurs when the commit you are merging in is a direct descendant of the commit you are currently on. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward because there is no divergent work to merge together.
results.rtfm_answer: During a fast-forward merge, Git simply moves the pointer forward because the commit to merge is directly ahead of the current branch. This means there is no divergent work to merge together, and Git updates the branch pointer to the latest commit, creating a linear history. [Source 2: progit.pdf (section: Basic Merging)]

results.question: How do you merge another branch into your currently checked-out branch?
results.expected_answer: To integrate changes, you use the git merge command followed by the name of the branch you wish to merge in. If the histories have diverged, Git performs a three-way merge using a common ancestor.
results.rtfm_answer:
To merge another branch into your currently checked-out branch, you can use the `git merge` command followed by the name of the branch you want to merge. For example:

```sh
$ git merge iss53
```

This command will merge the `iss53` branch into your currently checked-out branch. If there are any merge conflicts, Git will handle them and you may need to resolve them manually. After resolving conflicts, you can complete the merge with additional commits if necessary.

results.question: What is unique about a merge commit compared to a normal commit?
results.expected_answer: A merge commit is special because it has more than one parent. It represents a snapshot that results from a three-way merge of different development lines.
results.rtfm_answer: A merge commit is unique because it records the merging of changes from multiple branches. Unlike a normal commit, which represents a single author's changes at a point in time, a merge commit includes information about the branches being merged and the conflicts, if any, that were resolved during the merge process. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **Other Types of Merges**)]

results.question: What occurs if you change the same part of the same file differently in two branches being merged?
results.expected_answer: Git will encounter a merge conflict and will not be able to merge the branches cleanly. It adds conflict markers to the affected files and requires the user to resolve the differences manually before committing.
results.rtfm_answer: If you change the same part of the same file differently in two branches being merged, Git won't be able to merge them cleanly and will produce a merge conflict. You'll need to resolve these conflicts manually by choosing one version of the changes or merging the contents yourself. [Source 3]

results.question: What is the process of rebasing in Git?
results.expected_answer: Rebasing involves taking all the changes that were committed on one branch and replaying them on top of another branch. This operation rewinds the head to a common ancestor, saves diffs as temporary patches, and applies them in order on the target branch.
results.rtfm_answer: The process of rebasing in Git involves using the `git rebase` command to reapply commits from one branch onto another. This can be done to integrate changes from a topic branch into the main branch without merging, effectively rewriting history. For example, you can rebase a topic branch off another topic branch using `git rebase --onto`, or rebase a branch onto the master branch with `git rebase master server`. After rebasing, you might fast-forward the base branch to include the changes. However, rebasing commits that exist outside your repository and that others have based work on can cause issues, as it can lead to conflicts and require others to rebase their work, which is generally avoided to maintain a clean history. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **git rebase**)]

results.question: What is the primary risk of rebasing commits that have been pushed publicly?
results.expected_answer: The golden rule of rebasing is to never rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have based work on. Rebasing rewritten history that has been shared causes major confusion for collaborators who must then re-merge their own work.
results.rtfm_answer: The primary risk of rebasing commits that have been pushed publicly is that it can cause problems for your collaborators. Specifically, if you rebase and push commits that others have based their work on, they will have to re-merge their work, leading to messy histories when trying to pull their changes back in. [Source 1: progit.pdf]

results.question: How can you stop a rebase that is in progress and return to your original state?
results.expected_answer: If a rebase becomes too complex or you decide it was a mistake, you can run git rebase --abort. This returns your repository to the exact state it was in before the rebase command was started.
results.rtfm_answer: To stop a rebase that is in progress and return to your original state, you can use the command `git rebase --abort`. This will revert your repository to the state it was in before you started the rebase. [Source 1]

results.question: What is one major benefit of rebasing over merging when integrating changes?
results.expected_answer: Rebasing produces a cleaner, linear project history because it makes parallel work appear as if it happened in series. This is often preferred by project maintainers so they can integrate patches with a simple fast-forward.
results.rtfm_answer: One major benefit of rebasing over merging when integrating changes is that it results in a cleaner history. Specifically, when you rebase, the commits are replayed on top of a different branch, creating a linear history that appears as if all changes happened in series, even if they originally happened in parallel. [Source 1]

results.question: How do you register a new remote repository handle for your project?
results.expected_answer: You use the git remote add command followed by a shortname and the URL of the repository. This allows you to reference that URL easily using the shortname on the command line.
results.rtfm_answer:
To register a new remote repository handle, you can use the `git remote add` command followed by the shortname and the URL of the remote repository. For example:

```sh
$ git remote add pb https://github.com/paulboone/ticgit
```

This command adds a new remote named `pb` pointing to the specified URL.

results.question: What is the difference between fetching and pulling from a remote?
results.expected_answer: The git fetch command downloads all data from a remote project that you don't have yet but does not automatically merge it with your work. The git pull command is a combination of fetching and then automatically merging that remote data into your current branch.
results.rtfm_answer:
Fetching and pulling both interact with remote repositories, but they differ in their actions:

- `git fetch` retrieves new data from a remote repository without merging it into your local branches. It updates your local database with the latest information from the remote.
- `git pull` combines `git fetch` and `git merge` into one command. It fetches the latest data from the remote and then immediately tries to merge it into your current branch.

results.question: How do you push your local branch changes to a remote repository?
results.expected_answer: You use the command git push <remote> <branch> to share your commits. This only works if you have write access to the server and if no one else has pushed changes since your last fetch.
results.rtfm_answer:
To push your local branch changes to a remote repository, you use the `git push` command followed by the name of the remote and the name of the branch. For example, to push your local master branch to the origin remote, you would run:

```sh
$ git push origin master
```

This command calculates what your local database has that the remote one does not and then pushes the difference into the other repository, requiring write access to the remote repository which is typically authenticated. [Source 5]

results.question: What are remote-tracking branches?
results.expected_answer: Remote-tracking branches are local references that represent the state of branches on a remote repository at the time of your last communication. They act as bookmarks to remind you where the remote branches were last seen.
results.rtfm_answer: Remote-tracking branches are local branches in your repository that correspond to branches on remote repositories. They are created automatically when you clone or fetch from a remote repository and allow you to see the history of the remote branches locally. For example, when you clone a repository, Git creates a branch named `origin/master` to track the `master` branch on the remote repository named `origin`.

results.question: What are the three main sections of a Git project that files reside in?
results.expected_answer: Files in a Git project exist in the working tree, the staging area (also called the index), and the Git directory. The working tree is your local sandbox, the index stores information for the next commit, and the Git directory holds the metadata and object database.
results.rtfm_answer: The three main sections of a Git project where files reside are the working tree, the staging area, and the Git directory. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **The Three States**)]

results.question: What are the three types of objects Git stores in its object database?
results.expected_answer: Git's core data store consists of blobs, trees, and commits. Blobs represent file contents, trees represent directory structures and filenames, and commits store metadata and pointers to the root trees.
results.rtfm_answer: Git stores three types of objects in its object database: blobs, trees, and commits. Blobs store file content, trees represent directories and their contents, and commits point to trees and contain metadata about changes. [Source 1] [Source 2] [Source 3]

results.question: How does Git use the SHA-1 hash for data integrity?
results.expected_answer: Git checksums everything before it is stored and refers to it by that 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 hash. This makes it impossible to change file or directory contents without Git detecting the corruption or change.
results.rtfm_answer: Git uses the SHA-1 hash to uniquely identify each piece of content stored in the Git database. When you add content, Git computes a SHA-1 hash of the content and stores it as a file named with this hash in the `.git/objects` directory. This ensures that the content is immutable and can be reliably referenced and retrieved. The hash also helps in detecting any changes to the content, maintaining data integrity. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **Git Objects**)]

results.question: What is the purpose of the Git 'index'?
results.expected_answer: The index, also known as the staging area, is a file that stores information about what will go into your next commit. It acts as a proposed next commit snapshot that Git looks at when you run the commit command.
results.rtfm_answer: The Git index, also known as the staging area, is where Git stores information about files that are going to be committed. Specifically, it holds the content that will be included in the next commit, allowing you to stage changes before finalizing them with `git commit`.

results.question: What are 'plumbing' and 'porcelain' commands in Git?
results.expected_answer: Porcelain commands are the user-friendly subcommands like checkout or branch that users use daily. Plumbing commands are lower-level subcommands designed to be chained together or used in scripts to perform fundamental operations.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, "plumbing" commands are low-level, basic commands designed to be chained together or used in scripts. They provide direct access to Git's inner workings. In contrast, "porcelain" commands are higher-level, user-friendly commands that form the primary interface most users interact with daily. [Source 2]

results.question: Describe the Integration-Manager workflow commonly used with tools like GitHub.
results.expected_answer: In this workflow, every developer has write access to their own public fork and read access to the main canonical repository. They push changes to their fork and then send a pull request to the maintainer, who tests and merges the changes into the main project.
results.rtfm_answer: The Integration-Manager workflow, commonly used with tools like GitHub, involves contributors pushing changes to their own public repositories and then notifying the maintainer via email. The maintainer then merges these changes into the main repository. This allows contributors to work independently while the maintainer can integrate changes at their own pace. [Source 1]

results.question: What is a topic branch and why is it used?
results.expected_answer: A topic branch is a short-lived branch created for a single particular feature or bug fix. This technique allows developers to context-switch quickly and keep work isolated in silos until it is ready for code review and merging.
results.rtfm_answer: A topic branch is a short-lived branch used for a single particular feature or related work. It allows for quick and complete context-switching, making it easier to review changes and integrate them into the main branch when ready. This approach is particularly useful in projects of any size, enabling developers to work on multiple features independently and merge them as they complete each one. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **Topic Branches**)]

results.question: How does the Benevolent Dictator workflow operate for very large projects?
results.expected_answer: This hierarchical workflow involves 'lieutenants' who merge developers' topic branches and a 'dictator' who merges lieutenants' work into a master branch. Finally, the dictator pushes that master branch to a blessed reference repository for all others to use.
results.rtfm_answer: In the Benevolent Dictator workflow for very large projects, regular developers work on topic branches and rebase their work on top of the master branch from the reference repository. Lieutenants merge the developers' topic branches into their master branch. The dictator then merges the lieutenants' master branches into their own master branch and pushes this integrated master branch to the reference repository, allowing other developers to rebase on it. [Source 1: progit.pdf (section: **Dictator and Lieutenants Workflow**)]
